article.headline: Norway's Wealth Tax Sent the Rich Packing to Switzerland
article.lede: When Norway's Labour government raised the wealth tax to 1.1 percent in 2022, it expected extra revenue. It got a different result: a historic exodus of the country's richest citizens, most of them bound for the Swiss cantons of Zug and Lugano.
article.body:
For decades, Norway's *formuesskatt* — its annual net wealth tax — was the largely uncontroversial price of membership in one of the world's most equal societies. Then, in late 2022, the Støre government raised the top rate from 0.85 to 1.1 percent and simultaneously tightened the *upward adjustment factor* applied to dividends and share gains, pushing the effective capital-gains rate on equity income to roughly 37.8 percent. The combination was, for the country's wealthiest entrepreneurs, close to confiscatory: generating enough cash to pay a wealth-tax bill on paper assets often required selling shares, triggering a dividend or gains levy on top.

The response was swift and, by Norwegian standards, dramatic. More Norwegians with assets above ten million kroner left the country in 2022 alone than had departed in the previous thirteen years combined — 261 in 2022 and a further 254 in 2023, according to data compiled by the conservative think tank Civita from Statistics Norway records. Most headed for Switzerland: by 2024, roughly 300 ultra-wealthy Norwegians had resettled there, with smaller contingents in Britain, Monaco and Malta. The most conspicuous departure was Kjell Inge Røkke, once Norway's richest man, who moved to Lugano in September 2022 and had paid NKr181 million in tax the year before. Norwegian private bankers and wealth managers followed their clients; DNB, the country's largest bank, opened a representative office in Zurich.

The fiscal arithmetic is contested but not trivial. According to Norway's Ministry of Finance, the emigrants took with them NKr142 billion (roughly $13 billion) in *deferred income* — unrealised gains on shares and other assets that Norway may never collect. A broader estimate from Ole Gjems-Onstad, a professor at BI Norwegian Business School, puts the aggregate fortune of departing taxpayers at least NKr600 billion (about $57 billion). The government's own projections suggested the tax hike would raise NKr1.5 billion annually; instead, the emigration wave may cost NKr550 million or more in annual wealth-tax receipts each year, according to calculations based on Finance Ministry data. Total wealth-tax revenues have nonetheless risen — from NKr27 billion in 2022 to an estimated NKr34 billion in 2025 — because the levy's broad base (about 720,000 taxpayers, or one in eight Norwegians) more than compensated for losses at the apex.

The exit-tax rules introduced alongside the wealth-tax hike added a new dimension of friction. Before November 2022, an exit tax on unrealised gains expired after five years if the emigrant did not sell their assets — a relatively benign arrangement that allowed wealthy Norwegians to move abroad without an immediate reckoning. The Støre government abolished the five-year sunset, making the tax permanent until assets are actually sold or the taxpayer returns home. The change was partly aimed at closing a loophole; it also, somewhat predictably, accelerated the exodus by removing any incentive to wait and see.

Switzerland's appeal is not merely low taxes but *lump-sum taxation* (*Pauschalbesteuerung*), under which wealthy foreign residents pay a fixed annual sum based on their Swiss living expenses rather than their global income and wealth. Zug canton levies no cantonal wealth tax at all on individuals taxed under this scheme; Lugano, in Ticino, offers a mild Mediterranean climate and a culture that has long welcomed Italian and international money. For a Norwegian entrepreneur sitting on hundreds of millions in unlisted company shares — and facing a combined wealth-and-dividend tax burden that could exceed fifty percent on distributed income — the Swiss arrangement is not merely attractive, it is arithmetically overwhelming.

The episode has become a minor case study in *behavioural tax economics* — the branch of public finance concerned with how taxpayers respond to rate changes. The Støre government's critics argue the Norway experiment vindicates the standard prediction: above a certain threshold, a wealth tax does not so much redistribute wealth as relocate it. Defenders point out that aggregate revenues from the wealth levy have risen, that Norway's fiscal position remains robust, and that most of the country's wealthy stayed put. Both readings are partially correct, which is what makes the case instructive rather than decisive. Norway did not break its economy; it did hand Switzerland a windfall, and the debate over who got the better of that exchange will outlast the tax rate that started it.

concepts.definition: An annual levy on a person's net assets — the total market value of everything they own minus any debts — rather than on income earned during the year. Norway's version, called formuesskatt, applies at 1.1 percent to net assets above a threshold of roughly NKr1.7 million (~$160,000).

A tax triggered when a resident moves abroad, assessed on unrealised capital gains — profits on assets like shares that have risen in value but have not yet been sold. Norway's exit tax was made permanent in November 2022, meaning emigrants owe it whenever they eventually sell, with no expiry.

A Swiss arrangement, available to wealthy foreign residents who do not work in Switzerland, whereby annual tax is calculated not on global income or wealth but on a fixed multiple of the taxpayer's Swiss living expenses. It offers a predictable, often much lower, effective tax burden.

A Norwegian multiplier applied to dividends and capital gains from shares before the standard 22 percent income-tax rate is applied. With the factor set at 1.72, the effective tax rate on equity income reaches roughly 37.8 percent, designed to equalise the tax treatment of labour and capital income.

The study of how individuals and firms actually change their behaviour — relocating, restructuring assets, or timing transactions — in response to changes in tax rates, as opposed to simply paying more tax as the rate rises.

article.fact_check: The tweet's headline claim of '5,000 millionaires' leaving Norway for Switzerland is substantially overstated. Norwegian Finance Ministry data shows 82 wealthy residents (those with significant fortunes) left in 2022-2023; a broader measure using Statistics Norway's threshold of assets above NKr10 million (~$950,000) counts 261 departures in 2022 and 254 in 2023, totalling roughly 515 over the two-year period — and not all went to Switzerland. By 2024, cumulative Swiss-bound arrivals from Norway numbered approximately 300. The '100s of billions' figure is more defensible in NOK terms: the Ministry of Finance calculated NKr142 billion (~$13 billion USD) in deferred income left the country, while Professor Ole Gjems-Onstad estimates the total fortune of departed taxpayers at NKr600 billion (~$57 billion USD). Neither figure reaches 'hundreds of billions' in dollar terms, though NKr600 billion does. The tweet's numbers appear to draw on the most expansive estimates — possibly blending the broader Norwegian-kroner wealth figure with a loose definition of 'millionaire' that includes anyone with assets above a modest threshold — and then rounds aggressively upward. The core story is real and well-documented; the specific numbers are inflated.

poster_imidaily.blurb: Investment Migration Insider (IMI Daily) is the trade publication of record for the citizenship-by-investment and residency-by-investment industry — a niche that encompasses the programmes through which wealthy individuals obtain second passports or residency rights in exchange for qualifying investments or donations. Founded by Christian Henrik Nesheim, IMI Daily covers programme launches, regulatory changes, intermediary news and data on global wealth migration flows. It sits at the intersection of private wealth management, immigration law and sovereign fiscal policy, and its audience consists primarily of lawyers, advisers and programme operators rather than end investors.
poster_imidaily.credibility_note: IMI Daily is a specialist trade outlet with genuine domain expertise and broad sourcing across the investment-migration industry. Its reporting on headline migration statistics sometimes leads with figures from promotional sources (Henley & Partners, New World Wealth) that are not always independently verified; individual claims should be cross-referenced against official government data where possible. On matters of programme mechanics, regulatory changes and industry structure it is generally reliable.
